subject: Dedicated customer comms: performance profiles (versioning + pinning + expected behavior)

body:
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
To: Mateo Alvarez <mateo.alvarez@redwoodinference.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: 
Date: Wed, Feb 18, 2026 at 9:14 AM
Subject: Dedicated customer comms: performance profiles (versioning + pinning + expected behavior)

Hi all —

We’ve now had a couple of customer-facing questions land in Support/CS around “what changed” after runtime upgrades + how to stay on a known-good tuning configuration (SUP-22007 is the latest).

I put together a first pass of Dedicated customer messaging for the new hardware tuning profiles pack. Goal is to give customers:
- a simple explanation of what “performance profiles” are
- what they can expect to change (and what won’t)
- how versioning/pinning works
- how to request a change safely (and what info we need)

Request:
1) Technical sanity check (Mateo): is this accurate without over-promising?
2) Infra/SKU caveats (Neha): anything we should explicitly call out re: driver/CUDA variance + instance types?
3) Release/versioning language (Connor): make sure we match runtime-1.22 plan, default behavior, and any commitments.

Attached:
- Dedicated_Performance_Profiles_Messaging_v3.docx
- Dedicated_Performance_Profiles_FAQ_draft.md

Here is the draft copy inline (customer-facing):

---
## Performance Profiles (Dedicated): What they are
Redwood uses "performance profiles" to select a set of runtime tuning settings that are known to be stable and high-performing for your hardware (e.g., H100) and workload shape (prompt/response sizes and concurrency). These settings include batching/scheduling heuristics, memory/KV-cache headroom, and kernel variants.

## Versioning and why it matters
Each profile pack is versioned. A given version is a vetted collection of defaults we can reproduce and benchmark. When Redwood upgrades the runtime, we may also ship a newer profile pack.

## Pinning (staying on a known-good profile)
Dedicated customers can request that Redwood pins their deployment to a specific profile pack version.
- Pinning keeps the profile settings stable across runtime upgrades (unless you explicitly opt into a newer profile version).
- Pinning is reversible.

## Expected behavior by hardware
We maintain “expected behavior” guidance per hardware SKU (H100 / L40S / B200 preview) including:
- typical throughput vs. latency trade-offs at different concurrency levels
- memory headroom assumptions
- common failure modes and what signals to watch (e.g., queueing, kernel fallback rates, OOM/fragmentation)

## How to request a profile change safely
If you’d like to upgrade (or rollback) profiles, send us:
- your hardware SKU(s) and region(s)
- model(s) and context window
- typical prompt/response length ranges
- concurrency targets and latency SLOs
- any constraints (e.g., quantization, tool/function calling usage)

We will run an internal benchmark validation against representative workloads and schedule a staged rollout.

---

Open questions I’m not sure about:
- Do we want to state that Dedicated is “opt-in” for profile default changes, vs “case-by-case”?
- For B200: do we explicitly say “preview / early access only” in customer comms, or keep that internal?

Thanks,
Lauren

—
Lauren Bishop
Product — Dedicated
Redwood Inference



From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo.alvarez@redwoodinference.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Wed, Feb 18, 2026 at 11:02 AM
Subject: Re: Dedicated customer comms: performance profiles (versioning + pinning + expected behavior)

This is in good shape. A few technical tweaks so we don’t imply "magic" and so we set expectations on what pinning actually pins.

Edits / suggestions:

1) Define scope of pinning more precisely
- Customers are asking “will upgrades change my performance?”
- Pinning should be described as pinning the *profile pack version* (and optionally profile_id) used by the runtime.
- It won’t pin the entire runtime version. (i.e., bug fixes can still change behavior slightly.)

Recommended wording:
“Pinning keeps the profile selection and tuning defaults stable across upgrades. Runtime upgrades may still include bug fixes and kernel changes; we validate those against the pinned profile to prevent regressions.”

2) Avoid saying profiles are selected by workload shape unless we’re ready to expose that logic externally
Internally: yes (workload buckets). Externally: better to say “based on hardware and model characteristics; Redwood may adjust within safe bounds for stability.”

3) Add guardrails language
We should mention safety constraints:
- hard caps to prevent OOM and tail-lat blowups
- rollback path if SLOs regress

4) “Expected behavior” section: call out that it’s ranges, not guarantees
We can link the tables but keep the language as “typical” and “observed” under benchmarked conditions.

On Dedicated opt-in: I’d recommend we commit to “opt-in for any *default profile change*” at least for initial rollout of the profile pack. Runtime fixes are separate.

B200: I’d keep it out of customer comms except for customers explicitly in that EA. We don’t want support getting dragged into “when B200?” questions.

Mateo

—
Mateo Alvarez
VP Engineering (Runtime)
Redwood Inference



From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Wed, Feb 18, 2026 at 1:37 PM
Subject: Re: Dedicated customer comms: performance profiles (versioning + pinning + expected behavior)

+1 to Mateo’s notes.

Infra caveats to fold into the messaging (light touch):

- Hardware SKU matters (PCIe vs SXM, etc.). Customers often say “we’re on H100” but are actually mixed. We should ask for region + cluster ID / deployment name so we can confirm the exact fleet mapping.

- Driver/CUDA baselines: we have a baseline per SKU and sometimes exceptions during fleet transitions. We should not promise that “the same profile = identical perf across all regions” without those details.

Suggested line:
“Performance profiles are validated against Redwood’s supported driver/CUDA baselines for the target GPU SKU. If your deployment is on a non-standard baseline, Redwood will coordinate a safe migration plan.”

- On the “how to request a change safely” checklist: add “deployment mode (single region vs multi region)” and “burst patterns” since the scheduler/backpressure behavior is the main thing that customers notice at p99.

No need to mention B200 unless they’re in EA.

Neha

—
Neha Kapoor
Infrastructure & Reliability
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Dedicated customer comms: performance profiles (versioning + pinning + expected behavior)

Adding release/versioning notes:

- For runtime-1.22 we’re planning to ship profile pack v1.0 as the first “official” pack. Wording should be “profile pack v1.0” rather than implying we’ve had this forever.

- Version formatting: we should avoid “semantic versioning guarantees” in customer-facing docs. Internally we’ll keep a changelog, but customers should treat versions as: “v1.0, v1.0.1 hotfix, v1.1 feature update” (not strict semver). We can say “patch releases focus on stability/safety; minor releases may change performance characteristics.”

- Process language that matches what we can actually deliver:
  - Pinning is a supported request via Support/CS (not self-serve yet).
  - Rollback is supported and fast (hours), but not instantaneous for all deployments depending on maintenance windows.

- Please avoid stating “validated against your workload” unless we actually ran their workload. Better: “validated against representative workloads; we can run additional validation for your specific workload upon request.”

If you share the revised draft, I can reuse it in the runtime-1.22 customer upgrade note template.

Connor

—
Connor O’Brien
Release Engineering
Redwood Inference

Thanks — I incorporated all of this and tightened the language to avoid “workload-shape selection” details + to be explicit about what pinning covers.

Updated customer-facing copy (v4), paste below. If there are no objections by EOD tomorrow, I’ll hand this to CS to use as the baseline response for SUP-22007-like questions and we’ll also adapt for the Dedicated upgrade notice.

---
## Performance Profiles (Dedicated): Overview
Redwood uses a versioned “performance profile pack” to apply a set of vetted runtime tuning defaults for a specific GPU SKU (e.g., H100). Profiles include tuning for scheduling/batching behavior, memory/KV-cache headroom, and kernel variants.

These defaults are designed to improve predictability (latency/throughput) while maintaining stability and safety guardrails.

## Versioning
Profile packs are versioned (e.g., v1.0, v1.0.1). Each version is benchmarked against representative workloads and validated against Redwood’s supported driver/CUDA baselines for the target GPU SKU.

- Patch releases (e.g., v1.0.1) are focused on stability/safety fixes.
- Minor releases (e.g., v1.1) may change performance characteristics.

## Pinning (staying on a known-good profile version)
Dedicated customers can request pinning to a specific profile pack version.

Pinning means:
- Redwood will keep the profile selection and tuning defaults stable across future upgrades.
- Pinning is reversible and we can schedule a rollback if SLOs regress.

Pinning does not mean:
- Pinning the entire runtime binary forever. Runtime upgrades may still include bug fixes and kernel/runtime changes; Redwood will validate those changes against the pinned profile to prevent regressions.

## Expected behavior guidance
We maintain “expected behavior” guidance per hardware SKU describing typical performance and trade-offs observed under benchmarked conditions (latency/throughput, recommended concurrency ranges, memory headroom assumptions, and common failure modes).

If your deployment is on a non-standard driver/CUDA baseline or a mixed fleet, Redwood will coordinate a safe migration plan and set expectations for regional variability.

## Requesting a profile change safely (upgrade or rollback)
To request a profile change, please share:
- deployment name / cluster ID + region(s)
- GPU SKU(s)
- model(s) + context window
- typical prompt/response length ranges
- concurrency targets + latency SLOs (p95/p99)
- burst patterns / traffic shape (steady vs spiky)
- constraints (e.g., quantization settings)

Redwood will propose an upgrade plan (including staged rollout) and a rollback plan aligned to your maintenance window and SLOs.
---

Next steps I’ll take:
- Create a short internal CS macro version (1–2 paragraphs) and a longer “FAQ” version for escalations.
